h1:
Local Thai Food on Koh Chang
Stir-Fry, Noodles & Spicy Curry Rice
intro: Koh Chang is known for its beachfront seafood places at tourist prices, but the island also has plenty of local Thai spots where the people who actually work here — the songthaew drivers, the resort housekeepers — eat every single day for 50–90 THB a plate. That means hot made-to-order stir-fries, small bowls of noodle soup, and southern-style curry rice where you point at several dishes over rice. We've picked the best by main area, with the standout dishes and opening hours laid out straight.

blocks.html: Food prices on Koh Chang depend a lot on which area you're in. A single plate at a beachfront spot on the tourist side can run 150–250 THB, but walk back toward the road or into a village and you'll find the places islanders actually eat: made-to-order plates for 60–80, noodle bowls for 50–60, and two-dish curry rice for around 50–60 THB. Spicier, more generous portions, and open the hours real working people keep.

blocks.text: Southern curry rice — point, pile, spicy

blocks.html: Koh Chang sits in Trat province, but a lot of the curry-rice stalls on the island cook southern-style, because plenty of southerners come up here to work. Rich red curries, spicy stir-fries, dry southern curry (khua kling), sour curry — pick two over rice and you're set. It's the best value meal on the island. Go late morning to early afternoon for the full spread; by late afternoon the pots start running low.

items.name: Nong Anat Curry Rice (Nong Anat)
items.blurb: At the far end of Klong Prao village on the north side, this is the southern-style curry rice islanders pass along by word of mouth. Several pots to choose from for piling over rice, properly spiced and full-flavoured. A few foreign food bloggers have stopped by to film it. Genuine local prices — go a bit later in the morning and the dishes are still all there.

items.name: Raan Gaeng Som (Sour Curry House), Klong Prao
items.blurb: A small curry-rice shop on the Klong Prao roadside, best known for its sour curry and southern curries. Pick any two dishes over rice for one set price. This is where people working nearby grab a quick lunch.

items.name: Muslim stall, Klong Prao Bridge food court
items.blurb: A Muslim curry stall in the food court near Klong Prao Bridge, with proper fiery southern-style curries — massaman, chicken curry and more. If you like real heat, this is the one that hits the spot, and it's easy on the wallet.

blocks.title: Curry-rice tips
blocks.html: The good curries tend to sell out well before 3pm. If you want the pots still full, aim for somewhere between noon and 1pm. And most local shops take cash only, so bring small notes.

blocks.title: Want to taste deeper? Try a Koh Chang food tour or cooking class
blocks.text: Half a day with a local who knows the lanes — or cooking a dish yourself — teaches you more than just eating. Book ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide.

blocks.html: Made-to-order (tam sang) is the everyday meal for people on the island — pad krapao, fried rice, stir-fried curry paste, rad na, cooked the moment you order. Roadside and village shops charge 60–80 THB a plate, half the price of the beachfront side. Many stay open late, so they're your friend when hunger hits at night.

items.name: Gloy, Chai Chet
items.blurb: A small rice-over-curry and made-to-order shop around Chai Chet, packed with island workers at lunch. Single plates come out fast and the cooking has real flavour — one of the cheap spots locals get hooked on. It gets busy at midday, so arrive a touch before noon for an easy seat.

items.name: Took Ka Ta Kai Moon (Rotisserie Chicken)
items.blurb: A big place in the middle of Kai Bae, known for the rotisserie chicken turning out front. The Isan and made-to-order menu runs a full page — som tam, larb, pad krapao, all under one roof. Generous portions, great for a group.

items.name: Food court behind Morgan, Kai Bae
items.blurb: A multi-stall food yard in the centre of Kai Bae, with photo menus that make ordering easy — pad thai, noodle soups, curry rice. Walk around and pick from several stalls in one spot. It's the cheap-eats option in the touristy Kai Bae area.

items.name: Bird, Klong Prao
items.blurb: A worker-priced made-to-order shop around Klong Prao — fast, cheap, filling, and a go-to for people working in the area. Nothing fancy, but one plate and you're done. Good for a rushed meal mid-day.

items.name: Kapow, White Sand Beach
items.blurb: A small shop around White Sand Beach doing quick made-to-order plates — krapao, fried rice — at prices below the beachfront places on the same stretch. Good if you're staying at White Sand and want a real Thai meal without the markup.

blocks.text: Noodle soup — small bowls, light prices

blocks.html: Noodle soup on Koh Chang turns up at roadside shops and in food courts — clear broth, tom yum, and yen ta fo — for 50–60 THB a bowl. Some places do a loaded seafood tom yum egg-noodle for days when you want something heartier. It's a light meal for breakfast or before heading out on a snorkelling trip.

items.name: Noodle stalls, Klong Prao / Kai Bae food courts
items.blurb: Noodle stalls in the food courts at both Klong Prao and Kai Bae, with clear broth, tom yum and yen ta fo on offer, plus your pick of egg noodles or thin rice noodles. A small bowl is just right for a light meal — top up the condiments yourself to your own taste.

items.name: Seafood tom yum egg-noodle shop
items.blurb: A roadside shop reviewers often mention for its loaded seafood tom yum egg noodles — properly hot and sour. There's stewed pork-leg rice and made-to-order dishes to add on too. Basic bowls run around 40–50 THB. Worth it on a seriously hungry day.

items.name: 40-baht noodle stall, Ban Bailan
items.blurb: Around Ban Bailan–Lonely Beach there's a roadside noodle stall at about 40 THB a bowl, good alongside som tam and grilled chicken from the shops next door. It's the cheap-eats corner of the island's south side, where prices are still friendly.

blocks.title: Spice it your way
blocks.html: Local noodle shops usually set four condiments on the table — fish sauce, chilli vinegar, sugar, and dried chilli — so you can spice the bowl to your own taste. Southerners on the island tend to add a good amount of dried chilli and vinegar. Give it a go.

Beyond the sit-down shops, Koh Chang has local bites to grab on the go — roadside som tam and grilled chicken, morning moo ping with sticky rice, and dried seafood to take home. All much cheaper than ordering at a sit-down place.

items: Roadside som tam & grilled chicken — scattered from Klong Son down to Bailan, with som tam at 40–60 a plate and grilled chicken by the skewer or whole bird depending on size. Cheap and filling with sticky rice.
Morning moo ping & sticky rice — morning stalls around the villages and petrol stations, 10–15 THB a skewer. An easy breakfast before you head out.
Dried seafood — dried squid and dried shrimp, found around Ban Bang Bao and local markets. A handy souvenir to bring home.
Convenience stores + roadside stalls — on the Lonely Beach–Bailan side there are mini-marts and roadside food stalls open late, your fallback for a cheap dinner.

blocks.text: Eating local on Koh Chang — good value and safe

blocks.html: The local shops are spread along the road that loops the island, so getting to them means driving or riding a motorbike — and there are some real things to watch out for. Read this before you head off.

items: The ring road is steep with hairpin bends — especially the stretch from Kai Bae down to Bailan and Lonely Beach, where the gradients are severe. Inexperienced motorbike riders have crashes here often. If you're not confident, take a songthaew or call a ride instead.
Local shops take cash — most have no card reader or PromptPay. Carry cash in small notes.
Hours are unreliable in low season — during the heavy rains (May–Oct) some shops close early or shut entirely. Check ahead if you've got your heart set on one particular place.
You can ask for your spice level — local shops are genuinely spicy, so if you don't handle heat well, say 'phet noi' (less spicy) or 'mai phet' (not spicy) when you order.

blocks.title: honesty
blocks.html: If you're planning to take a boat out snorkelling around the nearby islands after breakfast, always check the weather first. During monsoon season the swell picks up and tours are often cancelled — don't pay in advance if the sky doesn't look right. And some accommodation on the island closes in low season, which can mean the restaurants near it close too.

faq.q: How much does local food cost on Koh Chang?
faq.a: The places islanders actually eat at are far cheaper than the beachfront spots: made-to-order plates 60–80 THB, noodle soup 40–60 THB a bowl, and two-dish curry rice around 50–60 THB. Beachfront seafood places on the tourist side start at 150 THB and up per plate.

faq.q: Where can I get spicy curry rice on Koh Chang?
faq.a: Many of the island's curry-rice stalls cook southern-style and properly spicy. We'd recommend Nong Anat curry rice at the far end of Klong Prao village on the north side, the sour-curry shop on the Klong Prao roadside, and the Muslim stall in the food court near Klong Prao Bridge. Go between noon and 1pm to catch the pots at their fullest.

faq.q: Do local Koh Chang shops take card or PromptPay?
faq.a: Most take cash only. The made-to-order, noodle and curry-rice shops in the villages usually have no card reader, so carry cash in small notes.

faq.q: Do I have to drive to the local restaurants on Koh Chang, and is it safe?
faq.a: The local shops are spread along the ring road, so you'll need a vehicle or motorbike — but that road is steep with sharp hairpin bends, especially from Kai Bae down to Lonely Beach. Inexperienced riders should take a songthaew or call a ride rather than riding a motorbike themselves.

faq.q: Are restaurants on Koh Chang open year-round?
faq.a: During low season (May–October) the rains are heavy, and some shops and accommodation close or keep unreliable hours. If you've got a particular place in mind, check ahead. The village shops where locals eat tend to stay open all year.
